CHAPTER 01 Java Core at a Glance The vocabulary every Java interview starts with, compressed into one page. THE FOUR PILLARS OF OOP PILLAR ONE-LINE MEANING Encapsulation Hide state behind methods; expose behaviour, not fields Inheritance Reuse and extend behaviour from a parent type Polymorphism One interface, many implementations, resolved at runtime Abstraction Expose what an object does, hide how STRING, STRINGBUILDER, STRINGBUFFER T YPE MUTABLE THREAD-SAFE USE WHEN String No Yes (immutable) Constants, keys, anything shared StringBuilder Yes No Building strings in a single thread (fastest) StringBuffer Yes Yes (synchronized) Rare; legacy shared builders EQUALITY /= compares references; equals() compares content. If two objects are equals() , they must return the same hashCode() . The hash picks the bucket, equals() confirms the match. Override both together, or neither. FINAL, FINALLY, FINALIZE KEYWORD WHAT IT IS EFFECT final Modifier Variable cannot be reassigned, method cannot be overridden, class cannot be inherited finally Block Always runs after try / catch , used for cleanup finalize() Method Called by the GC before reclaiming an object; deprecated, never rely on it final int MAX_SIZE = 10; try { process(); } finally { cleanup(); // runs whether or not process() throws } R E M E M B E R . Prefer try-with-resources over finally for closing resources, and treat finalize() as history.

WHY STRING IS IMMUTABLE CHAPTER 02 Why String Is Immutable Immutability means that once a String exists, its content never changes. Every operation that appears to modify it returns a new object. This is a deliberate design choice with seven payoffs. # REASON WHY IT MATTERS 1 String pool Equal literals share one instance. Mutation would corrupt every reference to it 2 Security Class names, file paths, URLs and credentials cannot be altered after validation 3 Thread safety No synchronization needed to share a string across threads 4 Caching Safe as HashMap keys and in internal caches 5 hashCode consistency Content never changes, so the hash can be computed once and cached 6 Class loading and interning Class names are strings; intern() only works if strings are stable 7 Simplicity Fewer side effects and fewer bugs HOW IT IS ACHIEVED The value is stored in a private final byte[] (since Java 9). There are no setters or methods that modify content. Every "modification" such as concat or replace returns a new String . WRITING YOUR OWN IMMUTABLE CLASS Declare the class final . Make all fields private final . Initialise fields only in the constructor. Provide no setters. Return defensive copies of mutable fields.

public final class Employee { private final String name; private final List skills; public Employee(String name, List skills) { this.name = name; this.skills = List.copyOf(skills); // defensive copy in } public String getName() { return name; } public List getSkills() { return skills; } // already unmodifiable } WHY THE DEFENSIVE COPY MATTERS Without it, a caller keeps a reference to the original list and can mutate the "immut‐ able" object from outside. The same applies to getters: return a copy or an unmodi‐ fiable view, never the internal collection. For collections, use List.copyOf() , Set.of() and Map.of() (Java 9+). They return unmodifiable collections and throw UnsupportedOperationException on modifica‐ tion. Collections.unmodifiableList() is only a view : if the original changes, the view changes. Watch out for mutable fields such as java.util.Date ; prefer LocalDate and LocalDateTime . I N T E RV I E W L I N E . Immutable objects are thread-safe by design, easy to cache, safe as map keys, and predictable to debug. Real examples: String , wrapper classes, BigDecimal , LocalDate , UUID .

CHAPTER 04 Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy A copy is a new object holding the same data as an existing one. The question is what happens to the objects it points to. Shallow copy copies primitive values and references . The original and the copy share the same nested objects. Deep copy copies primitives and also creates new instances of every referenced object. ASPECT SHALLOW COPY DEEP COPY Primitive fields Copied Copied Object references Same reference shared New object created Change to nested object affects original Yes No Speed and memory Faster, less memory Slower, more memory Safety Side effects possible Fully isolated SHALLOW COPY PROBLEM User u1 = new User(1L, "Ravi", new Address("Hyd", "500081")); User u2 = (User) u1.clone(); // shallow u2.getAddress().setCity("Bangalore"); System.out.println(u1.getAddress().getCity()); // Bangalore (u1 changed too) DEEP COPY, MANUAL @Override protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException { User cloned = (User) super.clone(); cloned.setAddress(new Address(address.getCity(), address.getPincode())); return cloned; }

SHALLOW COPY VS DEEP COPY DEEP COPY, VIA SERIALIZATION public static T deepCopy(T obj) throws Exception { ByteArrayOutputStream bos = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); new ObjectOutputStream(bos).writeObject(obj); ObjectInputStream ois = new ObjectInputStream( new ByteArrayInputStream(bos.toByteArray())); return (T) ois.readObject(); } WHERE IT MATTERS IN SPRING BOOT Caching: return deep copies from a cache so callers cannot corrupt cached state. API response DTOs: copy entities into DTOs so client‐side changes never leak back. Transactional safety: avoid unintended side effects on nested objects across ser‐ vice layers. Event publishing: publish copies of domain objects so consumers cannot mutate each other's data. R U L E O F T H U M B . Shallow copy is about performance, deep copy is about safety. Assignment ( = ) never copies an object, it copies the reference. Prefer immut- able objects and DTOs so you need fewer deep copies. Lombok's @Builder(toBuilder = true) produces a shallow copy, so nested objects still need manual handling.

CHAPTER 05 Interface vs Abstract Class Both provide abstraction, but they model different things. An interface is a contract: what a class can do. An abstract class is a base: what a class is, with shared state and code. FEATURE INTERFACE ABSTRACT CLASS Purpose Capability or contract Common base with shared behaviour and state Methods Abstract, plus default , static , private (Java 8/9+) Abstract and concrete Multiple A class can implement many A class can extend only one inheritance Constructors No Yes Instance No (only public static final Yes variables constants) State Cannot hold object state Can hold object state Access modifiers Methods are public by default Any: private , protected , public , default WHEN TO USE WHICH Use an interface when you define a capability that unrelated classes can have, ex‐ pect multiple inheritance of type, or want loose coupling. Think CAN DO : Runnable , Comparable , Serializable , Payment . Use an abstract class when related classes share state, constructors or protected members, or when you want default implementations and leave some methods to subclasses. Think IS A : Animal , Employee , AbstractList , InputStream .

INTERFACE VS ABSTRACT CLASS interface Payment { void pay(double amount); // abstract default void info() { System.out.println("Payment Info"); } static String getType() { return "Online Payment"; } } abstract class Employee { protected String name; protected double salary; Employee(String name, double salary) { this.name = name; this.salary = salary; } void display() { System.out.println(name); } // concrete abstract double calculateSalary(); // abstract } CAN INTERFACES REPLACE ABSTRACT CLASSES? Not fully. Interfaces can provide abstract, default, static and private methods. They cannot provide constructors, instance variables, mutable state, protected members or initialisation logic. DECISION TREE Do you need shared state (fields) or constructors? Yes → abstract class. No. Do you only need a contract or capability? Yes → interface. Neither fits cleanly? Reconsider the design. B E S T P R AC T I C E . Prefer interfaces for flexibility and loose coupling. Use ab- stract classes only when classes genuinely share code and state. Combining both is common: an interface defines the contract, an abstract class supplies the skeleton ( List and AbstractList ).

CHAPTER 06 The Exception Hierarchy Everything throwable descends from Throwable . The branch decides whether the compiler forces you to deal with it. Object Throwable Error / Exception → → BRANCH MEANING EXAMPLES Error Serious JVM-level problems; generally do not catch OutOfMemoryError , StackOverflowError , NoClassDefFoundError , LinkageError , AssertionError Checked: Recoverable IOException , SQLException , ClassNotFoundException , Exception conditions; must be caught or declared InterruptedException , ParseException Unchecked: Programming errors; NullPointerException , IllegalArgumentException , RuntimeExceptio no compile-time IllegalStateException , ArithmeticException , n enforcement ClassCastException , IndexOutOfBoundsException , NumberFormatException , UnsupportedOperationException , ConcurrentModificationException KEY POINTS Throwable is the root of the hierarchy. Only its subclasses can be thrown. Error represents serious JVM problems and is generally not handled. Exception represents conditions an application can handle. RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked. All other Exception subclasses are checked. throw new Throwable(); // valid throw new Exception(); // valid, checked throw new RuntimeException(); // valid, unchecked throw new Error(); // valid, but rarely appropriate R E M E M B E R . Use checked exceptions when the caller can realistically recover. Use unchecked exceptions for programmer errors and violated preconditions. Never catch Throwable or Error in application code.

CLASS LOADER SUBSYSTEM CHAPTER 09 Class Loader Subsystem The class loader subsystem prepares Java classes and loads them into memory. It works in three phases: loading, linking, initialisation . HOW SYNCHRONIZED WORKS INTERNALLY CHAPTER 25 How synchronized Works Internally synchronized gives two guarantees: mutual exclusion and memory visibility . THE MONITOR Every Java object has an associated monitor , like a lock. It tracks: Owner: the thread currently holding it. Entry queue: threads waiting to enter. Wait set: threads that called wait() . BYTECODE synchronized (lock) { // critical section } compiles to monitorenter , then the critical section, then monitorexit . The JVM en‐ sures monitorexit runs even if an exception occurs. LOCK ACQUISITION FLOW A thread wants to enter. Is the monitor available? Yes: acquire it and run the critical section. No: wait or block in the entry queue. On release, one waiting thread acquires the lock. REENTRANCY A thread can acquire the same monitor multiple times. The monitor keeps a hold count: Enter 1st (count 1) Enter 2nd (count 2) Exit (count 1) Exit (count 0, released) → → →

MEMORY VISIBILITY Changes made before monitorexit are visible to the next thread that performs monitorenter on the same monitor. This is a happens-before edge. WAIT() AND NOTIFY() wait() releases the monitor and moves the thread to the wait set. When another thread acquires the lock, changes the condition and calls notify() / notifyAll() , the waiter moves back to the entry queue, reacquires the lock, and continues. SLEEP() VS WAIT() THREAD.SLEEP() OBJECT.WAIT() Does not release the monitor Releases the monitor Thread keeps the lock while sleeping Thread joins the wait set UNDER THE HOOD (HIGH LEVEL) Fast path, CAS, no contention Contention rises: spinning / lightweight locking → High contention: thread parked by the JVM On release, a waiting thread gets the lock → → The exact implementation is optimised for performance and may vary between JVM versions. KEY POINTS synchronized is reentrant. It provides mutual exclusion and memory visibility. wait() releases the lock; sleep() does not. Always use while (condition) with wait() .

CAS: LOCK-FREE CONCURRENCY CHAPTER 26 CAS: Lock-Free Concurrency Compare-And-Swap is an atomic CPU instruction. It compares a memory location with an expected value and, only if they are equal, updates it with a new value. CAS(memory, expected, newValue): if memory /= expected → memory = newValue, return SUCCESS else → do nothing, return FAILURE PROPERTIES Atomic: the compare and update are uninterruptible. Lock-free: no thread waits for another to release a lock. Non-blocking: the system keeps making progress. Used for counters and concurrent data structures. TWO THREADS, ONE COUNTER Initial count = 10 . Thread A and B both read 10 and attempt CAS(10 → 11) . Thread A succeeds: count = 11 . Thread B fails: the value is no longer 10. It re‐reads 11 and tries CAS(11 → 12) . Result: 12, with no locks used. LOCK-BASED VS LOCK-FREE LOCK-BASED LOCK-FREE (CAS) Thread acquires the lock, updates, releases Thread reads, computes, attempts CAS Other threads wait Failed threads retry Risk: deadlock, blocking Risk: CPU spin under heavy contention

THE CAS RETRY LOOP while (true) { int oldValue = read(); // 1. read current value int newValue = calculate(oldValue); // 2. compute the new value if (CAS(oldValue, newValue)) break; // 3. try to swap // 4. failed: another thread changed it, so retry } This is optimistic concurrency : assume no conflict, detect it, retry. JAVA EXAMPLE class LockFreeCounter { private final AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(0); public void increment() { int current; do { current = counter.get(); } while (!counter.compareAndSet(current, current + 1)); } } In practice counter.incrementAndGet() does this for you. THE ABA PROBLEM Thread A reads value A. Thread B changes it to B and back to A. Thread A's CAS suc‐ ceeds even though the state changed in between. Solution: AtomicStampedReference attaches a version stamp: (A,1) → (B,2) → (A,3) , so the CAS detects the change. WHERE CAS IS USED AtomicInteger , AtomicStampedReference , LongAdder , DoubleAdder , and lock‐free stacks, queues and AtomicLong , AtomicBoolean , AtomicReference , non‐blocking algorithms. ONE-LINE ANSWER. CAS is a lock-free optimistic mechanism where a thread atomically compares the current value with an expected value and updates it only if they match; otherwise the operation fails and the thread retries. Best when contention is low; beware ABA and CPU spinning.

KEY FEATURES Reentrant: a thread can lock multiple times; it must unlock the same number of times. Fairness option: fair mode grants the lock to the longest‐waiting thread. Default is non‐fair (barging allowed). Interruptible lock acquisition. Timed and non-blocking acquisition with tryLock . Multiple Condition objects. TRYLOCK if (lock.tryLock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { try { /* critical section // } finally { lock.unlock(); } } else { // could not acquire: back off, retry or fail fast } CONDITIONS Unlike synchronized , which has one wait set per object, a ReentrantLock can have many conditions , for example notFull and notEmpty on a bounded buffer. COUNTDOWNLATCH VS CYCLICBARRIER CHAPTER 28 CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier Both coordinate threads; they answer different questions. CountDownLatch: "wait until a set of operations completes." Think of a count‐ down timer. CyclicBarrier: "everyone wait for each other at a point, then proceed together." The barrier can be reused. COUNTDOWNLATCH CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(3); Runnable worker = () /> { try { doWork(); } finally { latch.countDown(); } // always in finally }; new Thread(worker).start(); /* x3 // latch.await(); // main waits until count reaches 0 Key methods: CountDownLatch(int count) , await() , countDown() , getCount() . CYCLICBARRIER CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3, () /> System.out.println("All workers reached barrier")); Runnable worker = () /> { phaseOne(); barrier.await(); // wait for all 3 parties phaseTwo(); }; Key methods: CyclicBarrier(int parties) , CyclicBarrier(int parties, Runnable action) , await() .

COMPARISON FEATURE COUNTDOWNLATCH CYCLICBARRIER Purpose Wait until tasks complete Wait for all threads to reach a point Reusable No (one-time use) Yes (cyclic) Who waits One or more waiting threads All participating threads Counter Decreases to zero No counter; parties count Barrier action Not available Available (runs once per trip) Reset automatically No Yes, after all threads cross Best for One-time events, task completion Iterative tasks, phased coordination USE CASES COUNTDOWNLATCH CYCLICBARRIER Service startup: wait for DB, Redis, Kafka Multi-player game: all players ready, then start Aggregate parallel API calls Iterative scientific simulations Parallel file downloads then merge Matrix and image processing in phases Integration tests: wait for all components ML training: sync after each epoch IMPORTANT NOTES Always call countDown() in a finally block to avoid deadlock. If a thread waiting on await() is interrupted, InterruptedException is thrown. In CyclicBarrier , if one thread is interrupted or times out, the others get a BrokenBarrierException . For a dynamic number of parties or more complex phases, consider Phaser .

DEADLOCKS CHAPTER 29 Deadlocks A deadlock is a situation where two or more threads are permanently blocked, each waiting for a resource held by another. // Thread T1 // Thread T2 synchronized (lockA) { synchronized (lockB) { synchronized (lockB) { //. } synchronized (lockA) { //. } } } T1 holds A and waits for B. T2 holds B and waits for A. Neither can proceed. THE FOUR NECESSARY CONDITIONS (COFFMAN) All four must hold at once. Break any one and deadlock cannot occur. # CONDITION MEANING 1 Mutual exclusion At least one resource is non-shareable 2 Hold and wait A thread holds a resource while waiting for another 3 No preemption Resources cannot be forcibly taken 4 Circular wait A circular chain of threads exists, each waiting on the next COMMON CAUSES Inconsistent lock ordering, nested locks, long lock duration (holding locks during I/ O, DB or network calls), too many locks, and waiting on external systems while holding a lock. HOW TO PREVENT DEADLOCKS Consistent lock ordering. Always acquire locks in the same global order (A → B C), never B → A. Minimise lock scope. Keep critical sections small. Avoid nested locks. Refactor to reduce dependencies. Use tryLock() with a timeout. Do not wait forever; back off, retry or fail fast.

Use higher-level utilities. ConcurrentHashMap , atomic classes, Semaphore , BlockingQueue , CompletableFuture . if (lock.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { /* work // } finally { lock.unlock(); } } else { // timeout: retry or fail fast } HOW TO DETECT A DEADLOCK Take a thread dump ( jstack <pid> ). Look for threads in BLOCKED state waiting for monitors or locks; the JVM often prints "Found one Java‐level deadlock". Tools: jconsole , jvisualvm , Java Flight Recorder (JFR), IDE thread dump. DEADLOCK VS STARVATION VS LIVELOCK DESCRIPTION PROGRESS Deadlock Threads are blocked forever, waiting for each other No thread progresses Starvation A thread is continually denied access to resources Other threads keep getting resources Livelock Threads are not blocked but keep changing state in response to each other No useful work gets done REMEMBER THE FOUR CONDITIONS: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemp- tion, circular wait. Design for concurrency, not just correctness.

The fix depends on where the shared data lives. IN MEMORY TOOL USE synchronized Methods or blocks ensuring only one thread accesses the critical section ReentrantLock More flexible: tryLock , fairness, interruptible, timeouts Atomic classes AtomicInteger , AtomicLong for atomic operations without explicit locks Concurrent ConcurrentHashMap , CopyOnWriteArrayList , etc. collections IN THE DATABASE STRATEGY HOW Pessimistic SELECT //. FOR UPDATE locks the rows while updating locking Optimistic locking Version or timestamp column; check the version when updating; retry on conflict BEST PRACTICES Choose the right locking strategy for the use case and contention level. Minimise lock scope and hold time. Prefer optimistic locking for higher concurrency. Always handle retries and exceptions properly. Ensure proper indexing to reduce lock contention. K E Y TA K E AWAY. Race conditions occur when multiple threads or transactions access shared data simultaneously. Choose appropriate locking, in memory or in the database, to ensure data consistency and integrity.

CHAPTER 33 ThreadPool Rejection Policies A RejectedExecutionHandler decides what happens when a new task arrives but the pool and its queue are both full . WHEN IS REJECTION TRIGGERED? 2. 3. All threads in the pool are busy. The work queue is full. A new task is submitted. THE FOUR BUILT-IN POLICIES POLICY WHAT HAPPENS USE WHEN AbortPolicy Throws Banking, payments, order processing, inventory (default) RejectedExecutionException updates. Fail fast is better than silently losing work CallerRunsPolicy The submitting thread runs the task itself REST APIs, notification services, batch jobs, event processing. Creates backpressure; slows the producer naturally DiscardPolicy Silently drops the new task Metrics, logging, analytics, cache refresh, telemetry. Best-effort; losing an occasional task is acceptable DiscardOldestPolicy Drops the oldest queued task, then enqueues the new one Live dashboards, stock prices, sensor data, GPS tracking. Newest data is more valuable than older queued work WHICH POLICY SHOULD YOU CHOOSE? SCENARIO RECOMMENDED POLICY Payment service, order processing AbortPolicy REST API CallerRunsPolicy Notification service, email sending CallerRunsPolicy or custom Metrics, logging, analytics, cache refresh DiscardPolicy Live stock prices, sensors, real-time dashboards DiscardOldestPolicy Need retry, persist or alert Custom RejectedExecutionHandler CUSTOM REJECTION POLICY When you need to retry, persist, send to a queue, alert, or implement custom logic: class LoggingRejectHandler implements RejectedExecutionHandler { @Override public void rejectedExecution(Runnable r, ThreadPoolExecutor executor) { // Log, send to Kafka, retry, persist to DB, alert, etc. } } INTERVIEW TIPS AbortPolicy : critical operations. Fail fast. CallerRunsPolicy : best for most web apps. Provides backpressure. THREADPOOL REJECTION POLICIES DiscardPolicy : only for non‐critical, best‐effort tasks. DiscardOldestPolicy : real‐time workloads where the latest data matters. Custom handler: when tasks must be persisted, retried or redirected. R E M E M B E R . The right policy prevents system overload, data loss and cascading failures.

CHAPTER 36 Virtual Threads Project Loom, Java 21+ . Virtual threads make concurrency cheap while keeping the code simple and synchronous. THE PROBLEM Modern apps handle thousands of concurrent I/O‐bound requests. Platform threads are expensive, so one thread per request does not scale: High memory per thread (about 1–2 MB). Expensive creation and context switching. Many threads spend most of their time waiting for I/O. PLATFORM VS VIRTUAL THREADS ASPECT PLATFORM THREAD VIRTUAL THREAD Managed by OS / JVM JVM OS thread relationship Usually 1:1 Many virtual : few carrier (M:N) Creation cost High Very low Memory footprint Large (1–2 MB) Small (a few KB) Millions of threads Not practical Possible Blocking I/O Expensive (blocks an OS thread) Cheap (parks the virtual thread) Thread pool required Yes (usually) No (one VT per task) Best for CPU-bound work High-concurrency I/O-bound work HOW THEY WORK DURING BLOCKING I/O The virtual thread is running on a carrier thread (a platform thread). It hits blocking I/O (DB, HTTP). The virtual thread parks. The carrier thread is released to run another virtual thread. When the I/O completes, the virtual thread resumes on a carrier. Blocking a virtual thread does N OT block the underlying carrier thread.

VIRTUAL THREADS USING THEM ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); for (int i = 0; i System.out.println("Virtual: " + Thread.currentThread())); } executor.shutdown(); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() /> handleRequest()); VIRTUAL THREADS VS REACTIVE PROGRAMMING VIRTUAL THREADS REACTIVE Imperative, blocking-style code Non-blocking, async by design Easy to write, read and debug Built-in backpressure Use existing blocking libraries (JDBC, JPA, Excellent for streaming and event pipelines RestTemplate) Concurrency by making threads lightweight Requires a different mindset and APIs Best when: many I/O-bound tasks, you want Best when: streaming data, backpressure, simple synchronous code reactive end to end SAME LOGIC, THREE STYLES // Blocking + platform threads: simple, limited concurrency User u = getUser(); Orders o = getOrders(); Payment p = getPayment(); // Reactive (WebFlux): powerful, more complex Mono.zip(getUser(), getOrders(), getPayment()).map(t /> buildResponse(t//.)); // Virtual threads: same simple code, scales with high concurrency User u = getUser(); Orders o = getOrders(); Payment p = getPayment(); IMPORTANT NOTES Virtual threads do not make CPU‐bound code faster. The CPU is still the bottleneck. You still need limits for scarce resources (DB connections, HTTP connections, rate limits). Do not pool virtual threads. Create one per task. They are great for existing Spring MVC apps with blocking I/O. M E N TA L M O D E L . Platform threads: one request = one heavy thread. Virtual threads: many light threads scheduled on few carriers. Reactive: event-driven streams with backpressure. Different tool, same goal: handle more with fewer resources. Choose the right model for the problem, not the trend.

SPRING AOP CHAPTER 49 Spring AOP Aspect-Oriented Programming separates cross-cutting concerns from business logic. Cross-cutting concerns include logging, security, transactions, caching, exception handling and performance monitoring. "AOP is like a decorator magician who adds behaviour without changing the original code." TERMINOLOGY TERM MEANING Aspect Module that encapsulates a cross-cutting concern Join point A point during execution (a method call, etc.) Pointcut Expression that matches join points Advice Action to be taken at a join point Target The object being advised Weaving Linking aspects with target objects to create an advised object TYPES OF ADVICE ADVICE WHEN IT RUNS @Before Before the join point @After After the join point (always executes) @AfterReturning After successful return @AfterThrowing After an exception @Around Before and after; you control when to proceed HOW IT WORKS IN SPRING Client Proxy (Spring AOP) Aspect (advice) Target bean → → → The client calls the proxy , not the actual target. The proxy checks for applicable aspects (pointcuts). Advice is executed before/after/around the method. The proxy invokes the target method. Control returns through the advice. 2. 3. 4. 5.

EXAMPLE: LOG EXECUTION TIME @Aspect @Component public class LoggingAspect { @Around("execution(* com.example.service/.*(/.))") public Object logExecutionTime(ProceedingJoinPoint jp) throws Throwable { long start = System.currentTimeMillis(); try { Object result = jp.proceed(); return result; } finally { System.out.println(jp.getSignature().getName() + " took " + (System.currentTimeMillis() - start) + " ms"); } } } Enable with @EnableAspectJAutoProxy (Spring Boot auto‐configures it when AOP is on the classpath). All methods in the package and sub-packages within(com.example.service/.*) All classes in the package and sub-packages @annotation(com.example.LogExecution) Methods annotated with @LogExecution Combine with /& , /| , ! . PROXY TYPES JDK DYNAMIC PROXY CGLIB PROXY Default if an interface exists If there is no interface (or it is forced) Proxy implements the interface Creates a subclass of the target Only interface-based beans Can proxy concrete classes Uses java.lang.reflect.Proxy Uses CGLIB (Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB) Spring AOP is proxy-based and works at runtime , not bytecode weaving like AspectJ. SPRING MVC REQUEST FLOW: FILTER AND INTERCEPTOR CHAPTER 50 Spring MVC Request Flow: Filter and Interceptor How a request travels from the browser to your controller and back, and where filters and interceptors sit in that path. Client Servlet container (Tomcat) Filter chain DispatcherServlet → → → Interceptors Controller → → STEP BY STEP The client sends an HTTP request. The request goes through the Filter Chain ( doFilter ) at the Servlet level. DispatcherServlet (the front controller) receives the request and finds the hand‐ ler through HandlerMapping , then prepares the execution chain (interceptors + controller). Interceptors execute preHandle() in order. The controller handles the request and returns the response. Interceptors execute postHandle() in reverse order, then afterCompletion() . The response travels back through the filter chain (the finally portion of each filter). The response is sent to the client. FILTER VS INTERCEPTOR ASPECT FILTER (SERVLET) INTERCEPTOR (SPRING MVC) Level Servlet container Inside Spring MVC API javax/jakarta.servlet.Filter HandlerInterceptor Scope All requests (static and dynamic) Only Spring MVC requests Use cases Authentication, logging, compression, encoding, CORS, rate limiting Request logging, performance metrics, authorization, business checks

ASPECT FILTER (SERVLET) INTERCEPTOR (SPRING MVC) Can modify Yes (before and after) Yes (before and after the controller) request/ response Filter runs before and after DispatcherServlet ; it is part of the Servlet API. Inter- ceptor runs inside Spring MVC, around the controller. INTERCEPTOR METHODS METHOD WHEN preHandle(req, res, handler) returns boolean Before the controller. Return true to continue postHandle(req, res, handler, mav) After the controller, before view rendering afterCompletion(req, res, handler, ex) After request completion. Always executed NOTES Multiple filters run in order of registration ( web.xml or @Order ). Multiple interceptors run in order of registration ( InterceptorRegistry ). If any preHandle() returns false , the request does not go to the controller. afterCompletion() is always called regardless of success or failure of the hand‐ ler. EASY WAY TO REMEMBER Client → Filter DispatcherServlet Interceptor (pre) Controller → → → Interceptor (post) Interceptor (afterCompletion) → → → Filter Response → COMMON FILTER EXAMPLES LoggingFilter , GzipCompressionFilter , RateLimitingFilter , ExceptionHandlingFilter . AuthenticationFilter , CorsFilter , CharacterEncodingFilter , I N T E RV I E W T I P. A filter is outside Spring MVC (Servlet level). An interceptor is inside Spring MVC ( HandlerInterceptor ).

JSON TO JAVA OBJECT AND BACK CHAPTER 51 JSON to Java Object and Back How Spring Boot converts a request body into an object and a return value into a response. REQUEST FLOW: JSON → JAVA OBJECT The client sends POST /users with Content-Type: application/json and a JSON body. The servlet container (Tomcat) receives it and passes it through any filters. DispatcherServlet , the central front controller, receives it. HandlerMapping finds the matching controller method. HandlerAdapter ( RequestMappingHandlerAdapter ) invokes the controller. RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor detects @RequestBody . It delegates to a HttpMessageConverter chosen by the Content-Type . MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter uses Jackson's ObjectMapper . ObjectMapper.readValue(json, User.class) deserialises the JSON. The Java object is created and passed to your controller method. @PostMapping("/users") public User createUser(@RequestBody User user) { // business logic; `user` is already a Java object return user; } RESPONSE FLOW: JAVA OBJECT → JSON The controller returns an object. HandlerAdapter hands it to RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor , because @ResponseBody (implicit with @RestController ) is present. A suitable HttpMessageConverter is selected based on the Accept header and Content-Type . MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter calls ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString() . A JSON string is created and written to the HTTP response ( 200 OK , application/json ).

The response is sent back through DispatcherServlet and the servlet container to the client. KEY COMPONENTS COMPONENT ROLE Servlet container Receives the HTTP request (Tomcat / Jetty / Undertow) Filters Pre-processing: auth, logging, CORS DispatcherServlet Front controller; coordinates the whole flow HandlerMapping Finds the controller method HandlerAdapter Invokes the controller RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor Handles @RequestBody / @ResponseBody HttpMessageConverter Converts between HTTP body and Java objects MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter Jackson-based JSON converter (default) ObjectMapper The actual (de)serialisation engine ANNOTATIONS ANNOTATION EFFECT @RequestBody Convert the request body (JSON) to a Java object @ResponseBody Convert the return value (Java object) to the response body @RestController @Controller + @ResponseBody F LOW S U M M A RY. Request: Client → Container → Filters → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → HandlerAdapter → RequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor HttpMessageConverter → Jackson → Java object → Controller. Response: Controller → HandlerAdapter → processor → converter → Jackson → JSON → Client. Note that DispatcherServlet coordinates; it does not do JSON conversion itself.

CHAPTER 62 The N+1 Query Problem A performance problem where N additional queries are executed to fetch related data for N records . Example. Fetch all orders and their items: List orders = orderRepository.findAll(); // 1 query for (Order order : orders) { order.getItems(); // N queries (lazy load per order) } Total = N + 1 queries. Good: one query with a join. Bad: one query for the parents plus one for each child set. THE SEVEN TYPES PROPAGA‐ TION BEHAVIOUR WHEN TO USE REQUIRED Join the existing transaction if present, Most common. All operations (default) otherwise create a new one. The callee participates in the caller's transaction should succeed or fail together REQUIRES_NE Always create a new transaction. If one Audit logging, notifications, W exists, it is suspended independent operations that must commit regardless of the outer transaction SUPPORTS Join an existing transaction if present, otherwise run without one Read-only operations that can run inside or outside a transaction NOT_SUPPORT Always run without a transaction. An Operations that should not be part ED existing one is suspended of a transaction (reports, long- running tasks) MANDATORY Must run inside an existing transaction. If none exists, throw an exception The method must always be called in a transactional context NEVER Must not run in a transaction. If one exists, throw an exception Methods that must never be transactional (certain DDL, external system calls) NESTED Run a nested transaction inside the existing one using a savepoint . Rolling back affects only the nested part; the outer can still commit Partial rollback without rolling back the whole outer transaction

It only defines how a method participates. Rollback rules ( @Transactional(rollbackFor = //.) ) still apply. By default, un- checked exceptions trigger rollback ; checked exceptions do not. REQUIRES_NEW and NOT_SUPPORTED suspend the outer transaction, so ensure the connection pool is big enough (a suspended transaction still holds its connec‐ tion while a new one is acquired). Like all Spring proxy features, @Transactional is not applied on self-invocation: calling another method on this bypasses the proxy. BEST PRACTICES Use REQUIRED for business operations. Use REQUIRES_NEW for audit logs, notifications and outbox events. Avoid REQUIRES_NEW inside loops (it can exhaust connections). Keep transactions short and focused. Handle exceptions properly: unchecked exceptions trigger rollback by default. R E M E M B E R . Choose the right propagation to ensure data consistency, perform- ance and proper resource usage. Default = REQUIRED.

CHAPTER 64 Isolation Levels Isolation level controls how visible uncommitted or concurrent changes are between transactions. THE ANOMALIES ANOMALY DESCRIPTION Dirty read Reading data written by another transaction that has not committed yet Non-repeatable read Reading the same row twice and getting different results because another transaction modified it Phantom read Re-running the same query returns a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted rows Lost update Two transactions update the same row and one update overwrites the other THE FOUR LEVELS LEVEL DIRT Y READ NON-REPEATABLE READ PHANTOM READ LOST UP‐ DATE READ UNCOMMITTED Allowed Allowed Allowed Allowed (least isolated) READ COMMITTED Prevented Allowed Allowed Allowed REPEATABLE READ Prevented Prevented Allowed (varies by DB) Allowed SERIALIZABLE (most Prevented Prevented Prevented Prevented isolated) READ UNCOMMITTED: transactions can read data modified by other transac‐ tions but not yet committed. READ COMMITTED: transactions can only read committed data. REPEATABLE READ: repeated reads of the same rows return the same result. SERIALIZABLE: transactions execute as if one after another. Uses locks / range locks to ensure serial execution.

DATABASE DEFAULTS DATABASE DEFAULT PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED MySQL (InnoDB) REPEATABLE READ Oracle READ COMMITTED SQL Server READ COMMITTED N OT E S . The default isolation level depends on the database. Higher isolation means more consistency but may reduce concurrency. Use the minimum isol‐ ation level that satisfies your consistency requirements. Choose based on your use case: performance vs consistency.

CHAPTER 65 Pessimistic vs Optimistic Locking Concurrency control in database transactions. PESSIMISTIC LOCKING OPTIMISTIC LOCKING Philosophy Lock first. Assume conflicts will happen; lock the data when it is read Check first. Assume conflicts are rare ; let transactions proceed and check before commit Mechanism Row lock ( SELECT //. FOR UPDATE ) Version column (or timestamp) Concurrency Lower; others wait Higher; no locks while reading Consistency Strong Detected at commit time Downsides Blocking, risk of deadlocks, slower under load May require retry logic; not suitable for high-conflict data HOW PESSIMISTIC LOCKING FLOWS Transaction T1 starts and reads the data. T1 acquires an exclusive lock on Row A. T2 tries to read/write Row A and must wait. T1 commits or rolls back. The lock is released and T2 proceeds. @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) @Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.id = :id") User findByIdForUpdate(@Param("id") Long id); SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE; HOW OPTIMISTIC LOCKING FLOWS T1 and T2 both read the same row ( version = 1). Both modify the data in memory.

PESSIMISTIC VS OPTIMISTIC LOCKING T1 commits with version = 1: success , version becomes 2. T2 tries to commit with the old version 1: fails (version mismatch). T2 re‐reads the latest row (v = 2), applies its changes, and retries. @Entity public class Product { @Id private Long id; private String name; private BigDecimal price; @Version private Long version; // managed automatically by JPA } UPDATE product SET price = 120.00, version = version + 1 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 1; /- zero rows updated = conflict HANDLING THE CONFLICT IN JAVA try { repository.save(entity); } catch (ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException ex) { // reload with latest data and retry } WHEN TO USE WHICH PESSIMISTIC OPTIMISTIC Banking and financial transactions Read-heavy applications Inventory management Low-contention scenarios Seat booking / reservations User profile updates Critical updates where consistency matters E-commerce catalogues; any scenario more than performance where conflicts are rare K E Y TA K E AWAY. Pessimistic: lock when you read . Optimistic: check before you write . Use pessimistic locking for strong consistency and critical data; use optimistic locking for better performance and high concurrency with low conflicts.

THE PIECES PART ROLE Call stack Synchronous code is executed here and runs to completion Web APIs (browser) / native Handle async operations ( setTimeout , fetch , DOM events) outside the APIs stack Callback queue (task / Completed async operations queue their callbacks here macrotask queue) Microtask queue High-priority queue (e.g. promises); drained before the next macrotask Event loop Continually checks the queues; when the call stack is empty, moves the next callback onto it HOW IT FLOWS 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. Synchronous code runs in the call stack until it is empty. Async operations are offloaded to Web APIs. When an async operation completes, its callback is added to the callback queue. If the call stack is empty, all microtasks run first. Then the next callback from the callback queue is moved to the call stack. The loop repeats forever. One thread, many operations: the event loop never waits; it hands waiting to the system and picks the next ready callback. Block it and everything stalls, whether in Node.js, a browser, or a Netty event-loop thread.
